```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)

library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Srivastava 2017 ran linezolid dose-effect and dose-scheduling studies in the
hollow fiber system model of tuberculosis (HFS-TB) for sterilizing effect, and
then used Monte Carlo experiments to translate the hollow-fiber target into a
clinical dose. The paper contributes three models to nlmixr2lib:

* `Srivastava_2017_linezolid_hfs_aucmic`: the day-28 inhibitory sigmoid Emax
  curve of total *M. tuberculosis* burden against the free AUC0-24/MIC ratio
  (equation printed in the Results).
* `Srivastava_2017_linezolid_hfs_adr`: the day-specific quadratic curves of
  the linezolid-resistant subpopulation against %T>MIC (Figure 2C, digitized).
* `Srivastava_2017_linezolid`: the one-compartment oral population PK model
  of the Monte Carlo experiments (Table 2), with the paper's translation from
  serum to free epithelial-lining-fluid (ELF) concentrations.

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Srivastava_2017_linezolid"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1128/AAC.00751-17> (open access, PMC5527615)

```{r load-models}
mod_emax <- readModelDb("Srivastava_2017_linezolid_hfs_aucmic")
mod_adr <- readModelDb("Srivastava_2017_linezolid_hfs_adr")
mod_pk <- readModelDb("Srivastava_2017_linezolid")

# The two hollow-fiber models have no between-unit variability, so rxode2's
# notice about a multi-subject solve without omega carries no information.
solve_quiet <- function(mod, events) {
  withCallingHandlers(
    rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, returnType = "data.frame"),
    warning = function(w) {
      if (grepl("omega", conditionMessage(w))) invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
}
```

# Population

**Hollow fiber system.** Fifteen HFS-TB units were inoculated with
semidormant *M. tuberculosis* H37Rv at pH 5.8 (5.41 log10 CFU/mL at the start
of therapy; linezolid MIC 1 mg/L by three methods). Linezolid was dosed into
the central compartment to mimic the 4 h human half-life and the 3.3-fold
ELF:serum AUC0-24 penetration, at free AUC0-24/MIC values of 5 to 80 once or
twice daily and 111, 157 and 326 twice daily, plus non-treated controls. The
peripheral compartment was cultured weekly for 56 days, on plain agar (total
burden) and on agar with 3x MIC linezolid (resistant subpopulation).

**Human PK model.** This is not a cohort fitted by Srivastava 2017. The
authors took the mean and IIV of CL, V and ka from the population PK analysis
of Abe et al. 2009 in 435 patients (Table 2) and fed them to the ADAPT 5
PRIOR subroutine to simulate 10,000 adult tuberculosis patients for each of
150, 300, 600 and 1,200 mg once daily. Abe's covariate model is not reported
in Srivastava 2017 and is not encoded.

# Source trace

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Total-burden equation | log_cfu = E0 - Emax X^H / (X^H + EC50^H), X = AUC0-24/MIC | Results, day-28 equation; Methods, "Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling" |
| `le0`, `lemax`, `lhill`, `lec50` | 6.52, 5.62, 3.41, 79.46 | Results, day-28 equation |
| `mic` | 1 mg/L (fixed) | Results, first paragraph |
| EC80 check | 119 | Results and Abstract |
| Resistant-subpopulation equation | log_cfu_res = res0 + res1 X + res2 X^2, X = %T>MIC | Methods ("quadratic function of Gumbo et al."); Figure 2C |
| `res0_d*`, `res1_d*`, `res2_d*` (days 14-49) | per day | digitized by the maintainers from Figure 2C |
| PK structure | one compartment, first-order absorption | Table 2 (CL, V, ka) |
| `lcl` | 6.0 L/h (IIV 46.6%) | Table 2 |
| `lvc` | 54.53 L (IIV 25.9%) | Table 2 |
| `lka` | 0.58 1/h (IIV 40%) | Table 2 |
| `eta*` variances | log(1 + CV^2) | Table 2 footnote, "IIV ... as percent coefficient of variation" |
| `lrelf` | log(3.29) (fixed) | Methods, "Dose selection for optimal effect and minimal toxicity" |
| `fu` | 0.7 (fixed) | Methods, same paragraph ("30% protein binding") |
| Toxicity threshold | free serum AUC0-24 96 mg*h/L | Methods, same section |
| Residual SDs | 0 (fixed) | none reported |

# Hollow fiber total burden (day 28)

## Reading the printed equation

The Results print the day-28 fit as "effect (log10 CFU/ml) = (6.52 - 5.62) x
AUC/MIC^3.41/(AUC/MIC^3.41 + 79.46^3.41)". Taken literally, the bracket makes
the curve rise from 0 to 0.9 log10 CFU/mL with exposure, which is not an
inhibitory curve and cannot describe a burden that started at 5.41 log10
CFU/mL. The bracket is a typesetting slip for the standard inhibitory form
E = 6.52 - 5.62 x X^3.41 / (X^3.41 + 79.46^3.41), which this package uses.
The printed EC80 of 119 depends only on EC50 and H, so it checks those two
values but not the E0/Emax reading.

```{r emax-ec80}
emax_events <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5, time = 28, evid = 0L,
  AUC_LINEZOLID = c(0, 119, 1e6, 16.24, 73.60)
)
emax_sim <- solve_quiet(mod_emax, emax_events)
ec80 <- emax_sim$ec50[1] * 4^(1 / emax_sim$hill[1])
frac_at_119 <- (emax_sim$e0[2] - emax_sim$log_cfu[2]) / emax_sim$emax[2]
c(ec80_from_ec50 = ec80, fraction_of_emax_at_119 = frac_at_119)
stopifnot(
  abs(ec80 - 119) < 1,
  abs(frac_at_119 - 0.8) < 0.005
)

# The literal reading of the bracket tops out at 6.52 - 5.62 = 0.9 log10 CFU/mL.
literal_max <- 6.52 - 5.62
c(literal_reading_max = literal_max, inhibitory_reading_at_0 = emax_sim$log_cfu[1])
stopifnot(literal_max < 1, emax_sim$log_cfu[1] > 6)
```

The Results also name AUC0-24/MIC 16.24 as the exposure for bacteriostasis
and 73.60 for a 1.0 log10 kill. These are two of the hollow-fiber arms
(Figure 2A legend), not values derived from the day-28 equation; the curve
gives `r round(emax_sim$log_cfu[4], 2)` and `r round(emax_sim$log_cfu[5], 2)`
log10 CFU/mL at those exposures.

```{r emax-curve, fig.cap = "Day-28 inhibitory sigmoid Emax curve of Srivastava 2017 (Results). Dashed line: day-0 burden (5.41 log10 CFU/mL); dotted line: EC80 = 119."}
curve_events <- data.frame(id = 1L, time = 28, evid = 0L, AUC_LINEZOLID = 0:350)
curve_events$id <- seq_len(nrow(curve_events))
emax_curve <- solve_quiet(mod_emax, curve_events)
ggplot(emax_curve, aes(aucmic, log_cfu)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5.41, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 119, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Free AUC0-24/MIC", y = "M. tuberculosis burden (log10 CFU/mL)")
```

# Linezolid-resistant subpopulation (Figure 2C)

## Digitization check

Figure 2C draws one quadratic per sampling day without printing the
coefficients. Each curve was digitized from its pixels (axes calibrated on the
printed tick marks; data-point markers masked) and refitted with an
unweighted quadratic; the refits follow the drawn curves with a root-mean-square
error of 0.006-0.026 log10 CFU/mL. The table below holds a thinned sample of
the digitized curve points (one per 10% of %T>MIC where the curve is visible).
The packaged model must reproduce each of them closely.

```{r adr-digitized}
digitized <- data.frame(
  day = c(rep(14, 9), rep(21, 8), rep(28, 7), rep(35, 9), rep(42, 5), rep(49, 3)),
  ftmic = c(
    4.93, 14.79, 25.06, 36.36, 44.99, 64.91, 74.98, 86.48, 94.91,
    4.93, 25.06, 36.36, 44.99, 64.91, 74.98, 86.48, 94.91,
    4.93, 15.00, 24.86, 36.36, 44.99, 86.48, 94.91,
    4.93, 15.00, 25.06, 36.36, 44.99, 64.91, 74.98, 86.48, 94.91,
    4.93, 15.00, 25.06, 36.36, 44.99,
    4.93, 15.00, 24.86
  ),
  log_cfu_res_digitized = c(
    6.071, 6.117, 6.071, 5.932, 5.763, 5.193, 4.777, 4.237, 3.790,
    5.747, 6.225, 6.102, 5.855, 4.622, 3.713, 2.373, 1.248,
    6.487, 6.641, 6.564, 6.271, 5.901, 2.465, 1.341,
    5.840, 5.778, 5.609, 5.270, 4.915, 3.729, 2.943, 1.895, 1.032,
    1.017, 0.740, 0.478, 0.262, 0.139,
    1.695, 1.079, 0.586
  )
)
adr_events <- data.frame(
  id = seq_len(nrow(digitized)), time = digitized$day, evid = 0L,
  FTMIC_LINEZOLID = digitized$ftmic
)
adr_chk <- digitized |>
  mutate(
    log_cfu_res_model = solve_quiet(mod_adr, adr_events)$log_cfu_res,
    diff = log_cfu_res_model - log_cfu_res_digitized
  )
adr_chk |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(n = n(), max_abs_diff = max(abs(diff)), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::rename("Day" = day, "Digitized points" = n, "Max |model - digitized|" = max_abs_diff) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
# Model and points come from the same digitization, so the residual is pure
# digitization noise and a tight bound is appropriate.
stopifnot(all(abs(adr_chk$diff) < 0.1))
```

## Replicating Figure 2C

```{r fig2c, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 2C of Srivastava 2017: linezolid-resistant subpopulation versus %T>MIC by sampling day (quadratics digitized from the published curves, floored at 0)."}
grid <- expand.grid(day = c(14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49), ftmic = 0:100)
fig2c <- solve_quiet(mod_adr, data.frame(
  id = seq_len(nrow(grid)), time = grid$day, evid = 0L,
  FTMIC_LINEZOLID = grid$ftmic
)) |>
  mutate(FTMIC_LINEZOLID = grid$ftmic, day = factor(paste("Day", time), levels = paste("Day", c(14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49))))
ggplot(fig2c, aes(FTMIC_LINEZOLID, log_cfu_res, colour = day)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "%T>MIC", y = "Resistant M. tuberculosis (log10 CFU/mL)", colour = NULL)
```

On days 21 and 28 the curves rise to a maximum near 26% and 16% T>MIC before
falling, the inverted "U" the paper describes; on days 42 and 49 the
resistant subpopulation is small and falls to zero by about 60% and 40% T>MIC.
From day 14 to day 35 a %T>MIC of 100 gives the lowest resistant burden,
matching the caption's "A %TMIC of 100 suppressed the linezolid-resistant
subpopulation". The day-42 and day-49 quadratics turn up again slightly beyond
their visible range (about 0.1 log10 CFU/mL at 100%), an extrapolation of the
fit rather than a feature of the figure.

```{r adr-shape}
peak <- fig2c |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(
    ftmic_at_max = FTMIC_LINEZOLID[which.max(log_cfu_res)],
    at_100 = log_cfu_res[FTMIC_LINEZOLID == 100],
    min_value = min(log_cfu_res),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
peak
stopifnot(
  all(peak$ftmic_at_max[peak$time %in% c(21, 28)] > 10),
  all(peak$at_100[peak$time <= 35] <= peak$min_value[peak$time <= 35] + 1e-8),
  all(peak$at_100[peak$time >= 42] < 0.2)
)
```

# Clinical Monte Carlo pharmacokinetics

## Virtual cohort and simulation

The four Monte Carlo doses each get 200 virtual patients, dosed once daily for
seven days and sampled densely over the last dosing interval, when every
subject is at steady state.

```{r pk-sim}
doses <- c(150, 300, 600, 1200)
n_per_arm <- 200
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 144, by = 12), seq(144, 168, by = 0.5))))

pk_events <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(doses), function(i) {
  ids <- (i - 1) * n_per_arm + seq_len(n_per_arm)
  dose_rows <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = seq(0, 144, by = 24))
  dose_rows$amt <- doses[i]
  dose_rows$evid <- 1L
  dose_rows$cmt <- "depot"
  obs_rows <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = obs_times)
  obs_rows$amt <- 0
  obs_rows$evid <- 0L
  obs_rows$cmt <- "central"
  bind_rows(dose_rows, obs_rows) |> mutate(dose = doses[i])
})) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))

rxode2::rxSetSeed(20170725)
pk_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_pk, events = pk_events, keep = "dose", returnType = "data.frame")
```

```{r pk-vpc, fig.cap = "Simulated serum linezolid over the seventh once-daily dose (median and 90% prediction interval, 200 virtual patients per dose)."}
pk_sim |>
  dplyr::filter(time >= 144) |>
  group_by(dose, time) |>
  summarise(med = median(Cc), lo = quantile(Cc, 0.05), hi = quantile(Cc, 0.95), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dose = factor(paste(dose, "mg"), levels = paste(doses, "mg"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(time - 144, med, colour = dose, fill = dose)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time after the seventh dose (h)", y = "Serum linezolid (mg/L)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

## Closed-form check

For a linear model the steady-state dosing-interval AUC equals dose / CL. A
typical-value solve of 600 mg once daily must give 600 / 6.0 = 100 mg*h/L;
the solve is checked against its own closed form, so the tolerance is tight.

```{r pk-identity}
ss_events <- rxode2::et(amt = 600, cmt = "depot", ii = 24, addl = 13) |>
  rxode2::et(seq(312, 336, by = 0.05), cmt = "central")
ss <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_pk), ss_events, returnType = "data.frame")
auc_ss <- sum(diff(ss$time) * (head(ss$Cc, -1) + tail(ss$Cc, -1)) / 2)
c(simulated = auc_ss, closed_form = 600 / 6.0)
stopifnot(abs(auc_ss / 100 - 1) < 0.005)
```

## NCA with PKNCA

```{r pk-nca}
nca_conc <- pk_sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, dose) |>
  mutate(treatment = paste(dose, "mg"))
nca_dose <- pk_events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1) |>
  select(id, time, amt, dose) |>
  mutate(treatment = paste(dose, "mg"))

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(nca_conc, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(nca_dose, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 144, end = 168, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

nca_ind <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  select(id, treatment, auc = PPORRES) |>
  left_join(pk_sim |> distinct(id, dose, cl), by = "id")

nca_ind |>
  group_by(treatment, dose) |>
  summarise(median = median(auc), mean = mean(auc), sd = sd(auc), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(dose) |>
  select(-dose) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (once daily)" = treatment, "Median AUC0-24,ss" = median,
    "Mean AUC0-24,ss" = mean, "SD" = sd
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Steady-state serum AUC0-24 (mg*h/L) by dose, 200 simulated patients per dose.")

# Each subject's steady-state AUC must equal dose / individual CL (same draws,
# so only trapezoid and residual-accumulation error remain).
ratio <- nca_ind$auc * nca_ind$cl / nca_ind$dose
stopifnot(
  abs(median(ratio) - 1) < 0.005,
  quantile(abs(ratio - 1), 0.9) < 0.02
)
```

The paper reports a simulated AUC0-24 at 600 mg/day of 107.5 +/- 30.16
mg*h/L, against 91.40 +/- 39.3 mg*h/L in the US product label. The packaged
model gives the mean exactly from the log-normal CL distribution,
100 x exp(omega^2 / 2):

```{r pk-mean}
omega2_cl <- mod_pk |>
  rxode2::rxode2() |>
  (\(ui) ui$iniDf)() |>
  dplyr::filter(name == "etalcl") |>
  dplyr::pull(est)
auc600_mean <- 600 / 6.0 * exp(omega2_cl / 2)
auc600_sd <- auc600_mean * sqrt(exp(omega2_cl) - 1)
nca_600 <- nca_ind$auc[nca_ind$dose == 600]
data.frame(
  source = c("Srivastava 2017 Results", "Packaged model (closed form)", "Packaged model (200 simulated)"),
  mean = c(107.5, auc600_mean, mean(nca_600)),
  sd = c(30.16, auc600_sd, sd(nca_600))
) |>
  dplyr::rename("Source" = source, "Mean AUC0-24 (mg*h/L)" = mean, "SD" = sd) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
stopifnot(
  abs(auc600_mean / 107.5 - 1) < 0.05,
  abs(median(nca_600) / 100 - 1) < 0.1
)
```

The mean agrees to within 3%, but the paper's SD of 30.16 (CV 28%) is much
smaller than the 46.6% CV of clearance in Table 2 implies (about 51 mg*h/L).
The next sections show that the paper's own target-attainment and toxicity
results are consistent with the narrower spread; see Assumptions.

# Target attainment and toxicity (Figures 5 and 6)

The Monte Carlo endpoint is the free ELF AUC0-24/MIC at steady state,
`dose / CL x 3.29 x 0.7 / MIC`, compared with the hollow-fiber EC80 of 119.
Because CL is log-normal, the probability of target attainment has a closed
form, which avoids Monte Carlo noise in the comparisons below.

```{r ta-functions}
ini_df <- rxode2::rxode2(mod_pk)$iniDf
par <- setNames(ini_df$est, ini_df$name)
cl_typ <- exp(par[["lcl"]])
relf <- exp(par[["lrelf"]])
fu <- par[["fu"]]
sd_cl <- sqrt(par[["etalcl"]])

# P(free ELF AUC0-24 / MIC >= target) = P(CL <= dose x relf x fu / (target x MIC)).
pta <- function(dose, mic, sdlog, target = 119, relf_use = relf, fu_use = fu) {
  pnorm((log(dose * relf_use * fu_use / (target * mic)) - log(cl_typ)) / sdlog)
}
# P(free serum AUC0-24 >= 96 mg*h/L).
p_tox <- function(dose, sdlog) pnorm((log(dose * fu / 96) - log(cl_typ)) / sdlog)
```

## Figure 5: target attainment by MIC

At the MIC where each dose crosses the target, Figure 5 shows a target
attainment of about 0.47 (150 mg at 0.5 mg/L, 300 mg at 1 mg/L, 600 mg at
2 mg/L), and about 0.99 one MIC dilution lower. The first value is close to
0.5 for any spread, because these MICs sit where the typical patient's
exposure is close to the target; the second depends on the spread.

```{r fig5}
fig5 <- data.frame(
  dose = c(150, 300, 600, 150, 300, 600),
  mic = c(0.5, 1, 2, 0.25, 0.5, 1),
  point = rep(c("breakpoint MIC", "one dilution lower"), each = 3),
  figure5 = c(0.47, 0.475, 0.475, 0.995, 0.995, 0.995)
) |>
  mutate(
    packaged = pta(dose, mic, sd_cl),
    cv28 = pta(dose, mic, sqrt(log(1 + 0.28^2)))
  )
fig5 |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (mg/day)" = dose, "MIC (mg/L)" = mic, "Point" = point,
    "Figure 5 (digitized)" = figure5, "Packaged model (CL CV 46.6%)" = packaged,
    "Diagnostic (CL CV 28%)" = cv28
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
stopifnot(all(abs(fig5$packaged[1:3] - fig5$figure5[1:3]) < 0.05))
```

```{r fig5-curves, fig.cap = "Replicates the target-attainment curves of Figure 5 of Srivastava 2017 (EC80 target 119, packaged model, closed form)."}
expand.grid(dose = c(150, 300, 600, 1200), mic = c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)) |>
  mutate(pta = pta(dose, mic, sd_cl), dose = factor(paste(dose, "mg daily"), levels = paste(c(150, 300, 600, 1200), "mg daily"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mic, pta, colour = dose)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Linezolid MIC (mg/L)", y = "Probability of target attainment", colour = NULL)
```

## Figure 6: cumulative fraction of response and toxicity

The cumulative fraction of response (CFR) weights the target attainment by an
MIC distribution. The paper does not say which of its three distributions
(Spain, China, Germany) Figure 6 uses. The Spain distribution, read from
Figure 5 (243 isolates; proportions 0.025, 0.41, 0.515, 0.035 and 0.01 at
0.125 to 2 mg/L), reproduces the published EC80 CFRs, and is used here. The
toxicity endpoint is the proportion of patients whose free serum AUC0-24
reaches 96 mg*h/L.

```{r fig6}
mics <- c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)
spain <- c(0.025, 0.41, 0.515, 0.035, 0.01)
spain <- spain / sum(spain)
cfr <- function(dose, sdlog) sum(pta(dose, mics, sdlog) * spain)

fig6 <- data.frame(
  dose = c(150, 300, 600, 1200),
  cfr_figure6 = c(68, 96.5, 99.3, 100),
  tox_figure6 = c(0, 0, 14, 93)
) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    cfr_packaged = 100 * cfr(dose, sd_cl),
    cfr_cv28 = 100 * cfr(dose, sqrt(log(1 + 0.28^2))),
    tox_packaged = 100 * p_tox(dose, sd_cl),
    tox_cv28 = 100 * p_tox(dose, sqrt(log(1 + 0.28^2)))
  ) |>
  ungroup()
fig6 |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (mg/day)" = dose,
    "EC80 CFR, Figure 6 (%)" = cfr_figure6, "EC80 CFR, packaged (%)" = cfr_packaged,
    "EC80 CFR, CV 28% (%)" = cfr_cv28,
    "Toxicity, Figure 6 (%)" = tox_figure6, "Toxicity, packaged (%)" = tox_packaged,
    "Toxicity, CV 28% (%)" = tox_cv28
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
stopifnot(
  # Efficacy: the packaged model reproduces the Figure 6 EC80 CFRs.
  all(abs(fig6$cfr_packaged - fig6$cfr_figure6) < 5),
  # Toxicity: the packaged (Table 2) spread overshoots at 600 mg and
  # undershoots at 1,200 mg ...
  fig6$tox_packaged[3] > 20, fig6$tox_packaged[4] < 85,
  # ... while a CL CV of 28% reproduces Figure 6.
  all(abs(fig6$tox_cv28 - fig6$tox_figure6) < 5)
)
```

The EC80 CFRs match Figure 6 with the packaged model. For toxicity, the packaged model gives `r round(fig6$tox_packaged[3])`% at 600 mg
and `r round(fig6$tox_packaged[4])`% at 1,200 mg, against 14% and 93% in
Figure 6, while a CL CV of 28% (the CV of the paper's own simulated AUC0-24)
reproduces both. The paper's conclusions are unchanged either way: 300 mg/day
stays essentially free of the toxic exposure, and 1,200 mg/day reaches it in
most patients.

## Lower ELF penetration sensitivity analysis

Figure 6 also shows the CFR when the ELF:serum ratio is 1.52 instead of 3.29
(40.5%, 87.3% and 98.8% at 150, 300 and 600 mg). Replacing 3.29 by 1.52 while
keeping the protein binding gives much lower CFRs; applying 1.52 without the
protein binding comes closer.

```{r low-elf}
low_elf <- data.frame(dose = c(150, 300, 600), figure6 = c(40.5, 87.3, 98.8)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    with_fu = 100 * sum(pta(dose, mics, sd_cl, relf_use = 1.52) * spain),
    without_fu = 100 * sum(pta(dose, mics, sd_cl, relf_use = 1.52, fu_use = 1) * spain)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
low_elf |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (mg/day)" = dose, "Figure 6 (%)" = figure6,
    "ELF 1.52 x fu 0.7 (%)" = with_fu, "ELF 1.52, no fu (%)" = without_fu
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
stopifnot(
  low_elf$with_fu[2] < 70,
  abs(low_elf$without_fu[2] - low_elf$figure6[2]) < abs(low_elf$with_fu[2] - low_elf$figure6[2])
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Day-28 equation bracket.** The printed "(6.52 - 5.62) x ..." is read as
  "6.52 - 5.62 x ..." (see "Reading the printed equation"). The literal form
  is a rising curve with a 0.9 log10 maximum and contradicts the inhibitory
  sigmoid Emax model named in the Methods.
* **Only day 28 of the total-burden fits is encoded.** Table 1 ranks the PK/PD
  indices by AIC on every sampling day, but the paper prints parameter values
  only for the day-28 AUC0-24/MIC fit, the one it used to define the EC80.
* **Resistant-subpopulation coefficients are digitized.** The paper does not
  print the Figure 2C coefficients. They were obtained by a quadratic
  least-squares fit to the pixels of each curve, with axes calibrated on the
  printed tick marks. The day-42 and day-49 curves are visible only up to
  about 46% and 25% T>MIC before they reach the axis, so those two fits rest
  on the visible part. Figure 2C clips the curves at 0, and the model floors
  its output at 0 log10 CFU/mL to match. The day-7 curve, and a second flat
  curve in the same colour as day 14, both lie along the x-axis at about 0.1
  log10 CFU/mL and cannot be told apart, so day 7 is not encoded. The Table 1
  footnote says the resistant subpopulation was below the limit of detection
  on day 42, although Figure 2C draws a day-42 curve; the curve is encoded as
  drawn. The y-axis of Figure 2C is labelled "M. tuberculosis burden"; the
  caption identifies it as the linezolid-resistant subpopulation.
* **The resistant-subpopulation model is defined only at the sampling days.**
  The model picks the day's curve from the simulation time (cut points at
  17.5, 24.5, 31.5, 38.5 and 45.5 days), so values between sampling days are a
  step function, not an interpolation.
* **The resistant-subpopulation output name.** `log_cfu_res` is not in the
  compartment register, so `checkModelConventions()` reports one warning for
  `Srivastava_2017_linezolid_hfs_adr`. The same name is used for the same
  quantity by `Gumbo_2026_ethambutol_hfs`.
* **Transcriptome fits not encoded.** Figure 3 fits gene-expression levels
  (reads per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads) of
  protein-synthesis and efflux-pump genes against exposure, with no printed
  coefficients. They are descriptive bioinformatic fits and are not included.
* **Hollow-fiber PK not encoded.** The one-compartment fit of the hollow-fiber
  concentrations (elimination rate constant 0.17/h, half-life 4.09 h) is
  reported without a volume; it describes the device, not a patient.
* **PK model source.** Table 2 reprints the means and IIVs of Abe et al. 2009;
  the paper does not report Abe's covariate effects (body weight, age) or a
  bioavailability, so CL and V are apparent oral values and the dose enters
  the depot unscaled.
* **IIV as log-normal CV, and the narrower spread of the paper's
  simulations.** The Table 2 IIVs (46.6%, 25.9%, 40%) are encoded as log-normal
  CVs, omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2). The paper's own Monte Carlo output is
  narrower than this: the simulated AUC0-24 at 600 mg has CV 28%, and the
  simulated ranges in Table 2 (CL 2.03-18.2 L/h, V 42.1-69.9 L over 10,000
  patients) also imply a smaller spread than 46.6% and 25.9% CVs would give.
  The packaged model keeps the stated Table 2 values. As shown above, the
  efficacy results are insensitive to this choice, but the toxicity
  proportions of Figure 6 are reproduced only with the narrower spread.
* **ELF translation.** Target attainment uses the free ELF exposure, Cc x
  3.29 x 0.7 (`Celf`). The breakpoint-MIC target attainments of Figure 5 are
  reproduced only when both the ELF ratio and the protein binding are
  applied; with the ELF ratio alone the attainment at those MICs would be far
  above 0.5. The paper's lower-penetration sensitivity analysis (ELF ratio
  1.52, Figure 6 "EC80 with lower ELF-serum ratio") is not reproduced by
  replacing 3.29 with 1.52 while keeping the protein binding; it is closer to
  1.52 applied without the protein binding (see the section above), but the
  paper does not say which was done.
* **MIC distribution of Figure 6.** Not stated in the paper; the Spain
  distribution read from Figure 5 reproduces the EC80 CFRs and is used here.
* **No residual error.** None of the three models reports residual
  variability, so all residual SDs are fixed at 0.
